content.summary_of_the_paper:
### Overview

This paper aims to study complex networks with self-organization learning. 

In short, the major backbone of self-organization learning is based on related work on AAAI 2021 by Vargas and Asabuki. 

The dynamic system in a complex network is usually defined as a network control function by Barabasi et al; instead, the authors here use a transition matrix to model time series into probabilistic chunks and fixed chunk. 

In this work, the author further discusses learning based on dynamical equations and their applications in high-dimensional chunking. 

- Impact on the deep representation learning community:

When the authors only select a skip-gram word2vec from (Mikolov et al. 2013), there are some more advanced methods, such as network motifs, neural motifs, and node2vec missing in the current submission. I think the interest of this work is a bit disconnected from the major deep representation learning community in ICLR. 

- Impact on the complex network community

There are also some works tackling a learning-based function with self-learning networks (e.g., gene regulator network); the authors do not include, such as gradient-based GeneNet [A, B]. In terms of learning performance, some unique properties such as controllability are also good assessments for evaluating those complex networks. I encourage the authors could add some discussion on the stability of the learning-based network for discussion to enlarge their overall impact.

#### Summary

In general, the paper tackles a narrow problem with some weak representation learning baselines. When some network properties are not well studied with the proposed method, it is hard to actively recommend this paper for acceptance with relatively limited impacts to the ICLR community. 

*** 

**References**

A. Adapting machine-learning algorithms to design gene circuits." BMC Bioinformatics 20.1 (2019): 1-13.

B. Learning functions in large networks requires modularity and produces multi-agent dynamics, Workshop on Computational Biology, ICML 2018
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

- It is interesting to introduce a learning objection extended from the AAAI 2021 paper for the complex network learning community; although most of the baselines evaluated in this paper are limited. 

### Weakness

- The paper is with relatively weak novelty extended from the previous work [AAAI 2021]. 

- The general topic and applications are not clear, as the authors discussed in the paper. I am familiar with both complex network and deep learning literature. The simulated data used in this work is also not important complex network data, such as functional brain networks, e-coli networks, or gene regulatory networks. 

- the representation learning baseline is weak 


### Minor

Please use \citep or \citet for citations with better reading quality. The current setup, such as ".. problems Mayer & Jacobsen (2020)." is barely found out in any academic publication. 

- correct: "problems (Mayer & Jacobsen, 2020)." should be done on page 1

- more incorrect examples in the current submission: " Vargas and Asabuki Vargas & Asabuki (2021), " on page 3

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the problem of finding patterns in high-dimensional data (it seems mostly in sequential data?) via self-organization. The work presented seems to be an improvement of the previous SyncMap method, plus a new method to replace the previous dependency on DBSCAN clustering.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The authors tackle an important problem.
- The model comparison thoroughly investigates the effect of the diffent modifications (SyncMap vs SubSigma, and DBSCAN vs meta-variables)


Weaknesses:
- The paper is difficult to read due to language and flow.
- The introduction also makes many grandiose statements unrelated to the contents of the paper. For example, the entire first paragraph should be removed.
- The improvements to previous work are relatively minor, although the proposed evaluation shows that performance does improve.
- The evaluation, however, seems to be a bit biased. For example, the Variational Autoencoder used in the Word2Vec model only has a latent dimension of size 3, which is unrealistically small. A larger (and more common) value would probably perform much better.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is difficult to read due to some language issues. Improvements to previous work are relatively minor.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main limitations of the paper are its overall readability and the evaluation of the proposed method. I would consider the paper Borderline.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors introduce Magnum, which is an extension of a recently published method (SyncMap) that can more effectively deal with higher-dimensional problems. The proposed approach is compared with SyncMap and other methods on a series of synthetic sequence processing tasks denoted as “chunking problems”, where the goal is to detect the co-occurrence of states in a time series. The authors argue that the results suggest superior performance of Magnum.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
A strength of the paper is given by the accurate description of the model architecture provided by the authors. Moreover, the current framework is compared with the previous version (SyncMap) by highlighting the improvements made to the processing architecture to guarantee better scalability.

However, I also believe that the paper has several weaknesses:

- The present approach is strongly based on SyncMap (Vargas & Asabuki, 2021), which is described by the authors as a “state-of-the-art” method. I think this in an over-hyped description of SyncMap, since that model was only tested under very restricted conditions and is not considered a state-of-the-art approach in the deep learning community.
- The benchmark task (which was introduced in the context of SyncMap) is based on the analysis of time series generated according to a first-order Markov chain. I doubt this can be defined a “complex high-dimensional task”. The proposed method should also be evaluated on well-established benchmarks, which more faithfully reflect the complexity of modern sequence processing problems.
- The comparison with alternative methods might not be fair: for example, the Word2vec baseline was implemented with a latent dimension of 3, which is an extremely small number considering that normally the latent space spans a few hundred dimensions. The authors might argue that such choice was motivated by considering the map dimension of SyncMap and SubSigma (d = 3), but this choice appears arbitrary and could have a serious impact on the final evaluation.
- Why was the Word2vec implemented using a variational autoencoder? And how were the hyperparameters (especially the number of learning epochs) calibrated?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is readable, but the overall goal of the proposed approach is not very clear. The objectives of the proposed method should be put more clearly in relationship with existing methods (at present, the proposed approach is mostly compared to SyncMap). The relevance of the chunking task should also be highlighted, not only from a neuroscientific / cognitive perspective but also from a machine learning point of view. Moreover, while I acknowledge the importance of chunking in human cognition I wonder why the authors argue that deep learning models are missing such capability. In fact, even simple recurrent networks (implicitly) perform chunking when processing sequences (see, for example, the seminal work by Elman, 1990).

Quality: I think that the proposed architecture has some interesting features, but the paper appears quite narrow in scope and the evaluation procedure should be improved by including more challenging sequence processing tasks and by performing a fairer comparison with alternative models, as explained above.

Novelty: The proposed approach appears incremental with respect to recent work (Vargas & Asabuki, 2021).

Reproducibility: The authors do not mention a public code repository, but they uploaded the code as Supplementary Material. I did not look into it, but I guess this should allow for reproducibility.

References:

Vargas & Asabuki (2021). Continual general chunking problem and syncmap. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence

Elman (1990). Finding structure in time. Cognitive Science
content.summary_of_the_review: Although I see some merits in this paper, I think that its technical and theoretical contributions are not of sufficient quality for a top-tier conference such as ICLR.

content.title: Magnum: Tackling High-Dimensional Structures with Self-Organization
content.abstract: A big challenge for dealing with real world problems is scalability. In fact, this is partially the reason behind the success of deep learning over other learning paradigms. Here, we tackle the scalability of a novel learning paradigm proposed in 2021 based solely on self organizing principles. This paradigm consists of only dynamical equations which self-organize with the input to create attractor-repeller points that are related to the patterns found in data. To achieve scalability for such a system, we propose the Magnum algorithm, which utilizes many self-organizing subsystems (SubSigma) each with subsets of the problem's variables. The main idea is that by merging SubSigmas, Magnum builds over time a variable correlation by consensus, capable of accurately predicting the structure of large groups of variables. Experiments show that Magnum surpasses or ties with other unsupervised algorithms in all of the high-dimensional chunking problems, each with distinct types of shapes and structural features. Moreover, SubSigma alone outperforms or ties with other unsupervised algorithms in six out of seven basic chunking problems. Thus, this work sheds light in how self-organization learning paradigms can be scaled up to deal with high dimensional structures and compete with current learning paradigms.
